Q000853.stem: A 3 TB tabular training set in S3 is read by Athena for feature exploration (a few columns at a time) and by SageMaker training. Scans are slow and costly with CSV. Which format and layout fit BEST?

choices.text: One large Avro file so readers always get the full schema
JSON Lines with Snappy compression per record
Gzipped CSV, split into 1 GB files for parallel reads
Parquet, partitioned by a common filter column

Q000853.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet is columnar: queries read only the needed columns and skip row groups using statistics. Partitioning by a frequent filter (for example, date) prunes data further, and SageMaker and Athena both read Parquet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gzipped CSV: still reads every column, and gzip files aren't splittable.
• JSON Lines: row-based and verbose.
• One Avro file: row-based, and a single file limits parallelism.

Key takeaway: analytics-style reads → columnar + partitioned.

Q000858.stem: Data scientists, Athena, EMR, and SageMaker all need the same raw and curated datasets, with lifecycle to cheaper tiers and fine-grained table permissions. Which foundation fits?

choices.text: S3 data lake with Glue Catalog and Lake Formation
EFS as the primary store, with a copy per team in each account
One large EBS volume shared by all processing instances
An RDS database that stores every dataset as tables

Q000858.explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 is durable, low cost, and readable by all these services; the Glue Data Catalog provides shared schemas, Lake Formation manages table and column permissions, and lifecycle policies tier data by age.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared EBS: single-AZ and attaches to few instances.
• RDS: not built for petabyte raw files or ML training input.
• EFS copies: more expensive and duplicated.

Key takeaway: ML data lake = S3 + catalog + governance.

Q000864.stem: A data scientist wants to join S3 and Redshift data visually, apply 20 common transforms, see a quick-model feature importance, and then export the flow to a SageMaker pipeline without writing Spark. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue Studio with custom PySpark scripts
SageMaker Ground Truth with custom labeling jobs
SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon Athena with a set of saved SQL queries

Q000864.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Wrangler imports from sources such as S3 and Redshift, offers built-in transforms, data insights and quick-model analysis, and exports flows to processing jobs or SageMaker Pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Studio scripts: requires writing Spark.
• Athena queries: SQL only, no quick model or pipeline export.
• Ground Truth: labeling, not data prep.

Key takeaway: visual ML data prep → Data Wrangler.

Q000868.stem: A processing step must pass a small set of hyperparameters and schema metadata to a training step, readable by humans and by standard libraries, and diff-friendly in Git. Which format fits?

choices.text: JSON
A pickled Python object
RecordIO-protobuf
Parquet

Q000868.explanation:
Why this is correct:
JSON is human-readable, supported everywhere, and produces clear diffs, which suits small configuration and metadata files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parquet: built for large tabular data, not small configs.
• RecordIO-protobuf: binary training data format.
• Pickle: Python-only, not human-readable, and unsafe to load from untrusted sources.

Key takeaway: small config → JSON; bulk data → columnar/binary formats.

Q000870.stem: A numeric feature has 15% missing values, missing at random, with a skewed distribution and outliers. The model must not see information from the validation set. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Median imputation fit on training data only
Drop all rows that contain any missing value
Mean imputation computed on the full dataset
Replace missing values with zero everywhere

Q000870.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The median is robust to skew and outliers, and fitting the imputer on the training split only (then applying it to validation and test) avoids leakage. Adding a missing-indicator feature can also help.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full-dataset mean: leaks validation information and is skewed by outliers.
• Dropping rows: loses 15% of data or more.
• Zero: distorts the distribution unless zero is meaningful.

Key takeaway: impute robustly and fit preprocessing only on training data.

Q000871.stem: Sensor readings include rare extreme values: some are hardware glitches, others are real failure events the model must learn. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Flag outliers, keep real events, fix glitches
Remove every point beyond three standard deviations
One-hot encode the numeric sensor values
Min-max scale the data so outliers disappear

Q000871.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outliers aren't automatically errors. Investigate them with domain knowledge and rules: remove or correct glitches, keep genuine rare events, and consider robust scaling or clipping.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blind removal: deletes the failures the model must learn.
• Min-max scaling: doesn't remove outliers; they compress other values.
• One-hot numeric: inappropriate.

Key takeaway: outlier handling requires judgment, not a blanket rule.

Q000875.stem: A churn model uses customer age. Analysts believe risk changes in steps around life stages, and the model must be easy to explain per segment. Which transformation fits?

choices.text: Binning age into meaningful ranges
Tokenizing age into characters
Standardizing age with a z-score
One-hot encoding every distinct age

Q000875.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Binning converts a continuous feature into categories, capturing step-like effects and producing segments that are easy to explain.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Z-score: rescales but keeps age continuous.
• Tokenizing: meant for text.
• One-hot per age: very sparse and hard to explain.

Key takeaway: step effects and explainable segments → binning.

Q000880.stem: Product reviews must be turned into model input for a text classifier, and emojis and punctuation matter for sentiment. Which first step fits?

choices.text: Label-encode each whole review into one integer ID per unique review
Min-max normalize the review text length
Tokenize the text, keeping emojis and punctuation
One-hot encode each unique review string

Q000880.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tokenization splits text into units such as words, subwords, or symbols that models can map to vectors. Choosing a tokenizer that keeps sentiment-bearing emojis and punctuation preserves signal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Label-encoding reviews: every review becomes an unrelated ID.
• Length normalization: discards content.
• One-hot unique reviews: no generalization.

Key takeaway: text → tokens → vectors.

Q000882.stem: A team needs serverless Spark ETL that runs nightly, discovers new tables, processes only new files since the last run, and fails if data quality rules break. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Athena CTAS queries run on a schedule
AWS Lambda functions processing each file
AWS Glue jobs, crawlers, and bookmarks
Amazon EMR on a permanently running cluster

Q000882.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue runs serverless Spark jobs, crawlers discover schemas, job bookmarks track processed data, and Glue Data Quality rules can fail or route jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent EMR: servers to run and idle cost.
• Lambda: time and memory limits for large ETL.
• Athena CTAS: SQL transforms without bookmarks or rule-based failing.

Key takeaway: serverless Spark ETL with incremental loads → Glue.

Q000885.stem: New partitioned data lands daily in S3, sometimes with new columns. Athena and SageMaker need the tables updated automatically without breaking existing queries. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A manual ALTER TABLE run by an analyst each morning
A Glue DataBrew recipe applied to each new file
A Glue Studio visual job that rewrites the files daily
A scheduled Glue crawler updating the Data Catalog

Q000885.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas and add new partitions and columns to the Data Catalog. Their schema change policy controls how updates are applied, keeping tables current for Athena and other consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Visual job: transforms data but doesn't maintain the catalog by itself.
• DataBrew: data prep recipes.
• Manual ALTER: error-prone and slow.

Key takeaway: keep the catalog current → crawlers (or partition projection).

Q000886.stem: A team must label 500,000 images with bounding boxes at lower cost, using a private workforce for sensitive images and automatically labeling easy images. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels training
Amazon Mechanical Turk directly, without any labeling tooling
SageMaker Ground Truth with automated labeling
SageMaker Data Wrangler transforms

Q000886.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ground Truth supports bounding-box tasks, private or vendor workforces, and automated data labeling that uses active learning to label confident items automatically, reducing cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rekognition Custom Labels: trains models; it needs labels.
• Data Wrangler: data prep, not labeling.
• Raw Mechanical Turk: public workforce, unsuitable for sensitive data, and no automation.

Key takeaway: labeling at scale → Ground Truth.

Q000889.stem: A fraud model on data with 1% fraud reports 99% accuracy but catches almost no fraud. Which diagnosis and metric fit?

choices.text: Class imbalance; judge by recall, precision, PR-AUC
Label leakage; remove the most important feature
Underfitting; add more layers and train the model for longer
Data drift; retrain the model every week

Q000889.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With 1% positives, predicting 'not fraud' always scores 99% accuracy. Metrics focused on the positive class (recall, precision, PR-AUC) reveal real performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Drift: nothing indicates changing data.
• Leakage: would inflate fraud detection, not hide it.
• Underfitting: not indicated by the symptoms.

Key takeaway: imbalanced data → don't trust accuracy.

Q000892.stem: A dataset has 2,000 minority and 200,000 majority examples. The team wants balanced training without discarding data or overfitting on duplicates. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Remove the minority class and train one-class
Duplicate minority rows 100 times before splitting
Randomly undersample the majority to 2,000
SMOTE or class weights on the training split

Q000892.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SMOTE generates synthetic minority examples, and class weights make errors on the minority class cost more. Applying them only to the training split avoids leakage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Undersampling to 2,000: discards 99% of the majority data.
• Duplication before splitting: overfitting and leakage into validation.
• One-class: throws away labeled minority data.

Key takeaway: rebalance on training data only, preferring synthesis or weights.

Q000895.stem: A training dataset in S3 contains sensitive data. Security requires encryption at rest with a key only the ML team's roles can use, logged key usage, and encrypted training output. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-KMS with a CMK, set as the job's output key
S3 Versioning with MFA Delete on the bucket
S3 Transfer Acceleration so uploads use encrypted edge paths
SSE-S3 default encryption on the input bucket

Q000895.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer managed KMS key lets the key policy restrict usage to specific roles, with CloudTrail logging key use. SageMaker jobs can use a KMS key for output artifacts and volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3: encrypts, but no key-level access control or usage logs.
• Versioning/MFA Delete: protect against deletion, not reading.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed only.

Key takeaway: control who can decrypt → a customer managed key.

Q000898.stem: A US health app's ML team processes diagnosis codes and claims linked to patients, and the company is a HIPAA covered entity. What does this data category require on AWS?

choices.text: PHI: BAA, eligible services, encryption
It's anonymous statistics, since codes aren't names
It's public data, so no special handling is needed
It's regulated only if stored outside the US

Q000898.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Health data linked to individuals is protected health information. On AWS, covered entities sign a BAA, use HIPAA-eligible services, and apply safeguards such as encryption, access control, and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public or anonymous: codes linked to patients identify health information.
• Location-based: HIPAA applies regardless of storage location.

Key takeaway: PHI → BAA + eligible services + safeguards.

Q000901.stem: A lender must explain individual predictions to regulators and check whether approval rates differ across age groups before and after training. Which tool fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Debugger
SageMaker Model Monitor data quality
Amazon Comprehend
SageMaker Clarify

Q000901.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify computes pre- and post-training bias metrics and feature attributions (SHAP) for individual predictions, and can monitor both in production with Model Monitor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Debugger: training internals such as gradients.
• Data quality monitor: distribution drift, not bias or explanations.
• Comprehend: text analytics.

Key takeaway: bias + explainability → Clarify.

Q000903.stem: A pipeline must stop before training if more than 1% of rows have null customer IDs or if the label column has unexpected values. Which approach fits with the least code?

choices.text: Glue Data Quality rules (DQDL) as a pipeline gate
CloudWatch alarms on the S3 bucket's size and object count
Manual checks in a notebook before each run
Model Monitor data quality on the training data

Q000903.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Data Quality lets you declare rules such as completeness and allowed values in DQDL and act on results, failing jobs or routing data, before training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual checks: not automated.
• Model Monitor: monitors endpoints, not pipeline gates.
• Bucket size: says nothing about data quality.

Key takeaway: declarative data checks → Glue Data Quality.

Q000905.stem: A churn model uses 80 numeric and categorical features on 2 million rows. The team needs strong accuracy quickly, handling of missing values, and feature importance. Which algorithm fits BEST as a first choice?

choices.text: A deep convolutional neural network
SageMaker XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees)
K-means clustering on the features to find churners
DeepAR forecasting

Q000905.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost are strong baselines for tabular data, handle missing values natively, and provide feature importance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNN: designed for images.
• K-means: unsupervised; it doesn't predict churn.
• DeepAR: time-series forecasting.

Key takeaway: tabular supervised → gradient-boosted trees first.

Q000908.stem: An app must translate support tickets into English in real time and apply company-specific terms consistently (product names must not be translated). Which approach fits?

choices.text: Amazon Comprehend with custom entity recognition
Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabularies
A seq2seq model trained from scratch on SageMaker
Amazon Translate with custom terminology

Q000908.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Translate provides real-time neural translation, and custom terminology keeps specific terms, such as product names, translated (or untranslated) exactly as defined.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend: analysis, not translation.
• Transcribe: speech to text.
• Training from scratch: slow and costly.

Key takeaway: translation with controlled terms → Translate + custom terminology.

Q000912.stem: A team wants to try several pretrained open models for text classification, fine-tune one on its data, and deploy it with one click, in its own account. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker JumpStart
SageMaker Neo

Q000912.explanation:
Why this is correct:
JumpStart provides a catalog of pretrained models and solution templates that can be fine-tuned and deployed to endpoints in your account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Feature Store: features.
• Neo: compilation for hardware.

Key takeaway: pretrained model catalog + fine-tune + deploy → JumpStart.

Q000917.stem: A retailer must forecast demand for 20,000 related products, including new products with little history, and provide prediction intervals for inventory planning. Which approach fits?

choices.text: DeepAR with quantile forecasts
K-means clustering of historical sales
XGBoost predicting only point estimates
A separate linear regression per product

Q000917.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DeepAR trains one model across many related time series, which helps cold-start items, and produces probabilistic (quantile) forecasts for intervals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-product regression: poor for sparse or new items and no intervals.
• K-means: groups items; doesn't forecast.
• Point estimates only: no intervals.

Key takeaway: many related series + intervals → DeepAR.

Q000920.stem: A factory needs to know which of 12 defect types appear anywhere in an image (several can appear at once), without locating them. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Object detection with bounding boxes
Semantic segmentation per pixel
BlazingText on image file names
Multi-label image classification

Q000920.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image classification assigns labels to the whole image, and multi-label mode supports several labels per image. Locations aren't required here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object detection: adds localization that isn't needed.
• Segmentation: pixel-level, even more than needed.
• BlazingText: for text.

Key takeaway: what's in the image (no location) → classification.

Q000921.stem: Training uses 1,000,000 examples with batch size 500 for 10 epochs. How many weight updates occur, and what is one epoch?

choices.text: 2,000 updates; an epoch is one layer
10 updates; an epoch is one weight update
500 updates; an epoch is one batch
20,000 updates; an epoch is one full pass

Q000921.explanation:
Why this is correct:
One epoch processes the full dataset once. Here that's 1,000,000 / 500 = 2,000 batches (updates) per epoch, so 10 epochs give 20,000 updates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One update per epoch: that would be full-batch training.
• One batch per epoch: confuses batch with epoch.
• Layer-based: epochs aren't related to layers.

Key takeaway: updates = (examples / batch size) × epochs.

Q000923.stem: Validation loss stops improving after epoch 12 of 100, and training continues to reduce training loss. The team wants to save cost and keep the best model. Which technique fits?

choices.text: More training epochs to reach convergence
A higher learning rate for the final epochs to escape the plateau
Early stopping with checkpoint of the best epoch
Removing the validation set to use more data

Q000923.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Early stopping ends training when the validation metric stops improving for a set patience, saving compute and avoiding overfitting. Keeping the best checkpoint retains the best model. SageMaker tuning jobs can also stop weak jobs early.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher learning rate: likely worsens things.
• More epochs: more overfitting and cost.
• No validation set: loses the stopping signal.

Key takeaway: stop on validation plateau; keep the best checkpoint.

Q000925.stem: A large neural network overfits: 99% training accuracy, 78% validation. The team wants a regularization technique applied during training that randomly disables neurons. Which is it, and when is it active?

choices.text: Data augmentation, applied to the weights
Dropout, active only during training
Early stopping, applied to individual neurons
Batch normalization, active only during inference

Q000925.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training, which forces redundancy and reduces overfitting. At inference, all neurons are used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch normalization: normalizes activations; not random deactivation.
• Early stopping: stops training; not per neuron.
• Data augmentation: changes input data, not weights.

Key takeaway: dropout = training-time random deactivation.

Q000929.stem: A team has a PyTorch training script with a custom loop and wants to run it on SageMaker with managed spot training and distributed data parallelism, without building a container. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Autopilot with the script uploaded
A custom Docker image built from scratch
A SageMaker built-in algorithm that replaces the script
Script mode with the SageMaker PyTorch container

Q000929.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Script mode runs your own training script in a prebuilt framework container, with SageMaker features such as spot training and distribution configured through the estimator.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Built-in algorithm: discards the custom code.
• Autopilot: AutoML; doesn't run your script.
• Custom image: unnecessary work here.

Key takeaway: own script + managed framework container → script mode.

Q000935.stem: Models must be versioned, approved by a reviewer, and deployed automatically only when approved, with lineage to the training job. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Feature Store
An S3 bucket with a folder per model version
Amazon ECR image tags
Model Registry with approval status

Q000935.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Registry groups model versions (model packages) with metadata and lineage. Approval status changes emit events that can trigger deployment pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 folders: no approval workflow.
• Feature Store: features, not models.
• ECR tags: images, not model approval.

Key takeaway: versioned, approved models → Model Registry.

Q000936.stem: A model's weights grow very large and it overfits. The team adds a term to the loss equal to λ times the sum of squared weights. What is this, and what is its effect?

choices.text: L2 regularization (weight decay); smaller weights
Dropout; disables neurons at random
Learning rate decay; slows training over time
L1 regularization; forces weights to exactly zero

Q000936.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weight decay (L2) penalizes squared weights, shrinking them and reducing overfitting. L1 penalizes absolute values and tends to produce sparse weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• L1: absolute-value penalty.
• Dropout: random deactivation, not a loss term.
• Learning rate decay: changes step size, not the loss.

Key takeaway: squared penalty = L2; absolute = L1.

Q000939.stem: A spam classifier must balance false positives (lost emails) and false negatives (spam getting through) with one metric for model selection, on imbalanced data. Which metric fits?

choices.text: F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall)
R-squared of the predicted probabilities
Accuracy on the full test set, including both classes
RMSE of the predicted probabilities

Q000939.explanation:
Why this is correct:
F1 combines precision and recall, and the harmonic mean penalizes a model that is strong on one but weak on the other. It suits imbalanced classification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy: misleading with imbalance.
• RMSE and R-squared: regression metrics.

Key takeaway: one number balancing precision and recall → F1.

Q000940.stem: A disease screening model flags 50 healthy patients as sick. What are these errors called, and which metric do they lower?

choices.text: False negatives; they lower recall
True positives; they lower accuracy
True negatives; they lower specificity
False positives; they lower precision

Q000940.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Healthy people predicted positive are false positives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP), so more false positives lower precision.

Why the other options are wrong:
• False negatives: sick patients predicted healthy, which lower recall.
• True negatives: correct predictions.
• True positives: correct predictions.

Key takeaway: FP → precision; FN → recall.

Q000941.stem: A delivery-time model will be judged mainly on avoiding large errors, since a few very late deliveries cost far more than many small errors. Which metric fits BEST?

choices.text: RMSE, which penalizes large errors more
MAE, which weighs every error equally regardless of size
AUC-ROC of the predictions
Accuracy of rounded predictions

Q000941.explanation:
Why this is correct:
RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large errors dominate the score. MAE treats all errors linearly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MAE: doesn't emphasize large errors.
• Accuracy and AUC: classification metrics.

Key takeaway: large errors costly → RMSE.

Q000946.stem: A deep training job occasionally diverges with exploding gradients after hours of compute. The team wants it detected automatically and the job stopped early to save cost. Which fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail events for the training job's API calls
Clarify bias reports on the model
Model Monitor schedules on the endpoint
Debugger built-in rules with a stop action

Q000946.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Debugger captures tensors during training and evaluates rules such as exploding gradients or overfitting. Rule actions can stop the job and notify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias and explainability.
• Model Monitor: production endpoints.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: training health checks → Debugger rules.

Q000948.stem: A complex model reports 91% accuracy on a dataset where 90% of examples are one class. How should the team interpret this?

choices.text: Use the complex model as the baseline
91% shows the model is production-ready
Baselines are only needed for regression models, not classifiers
Compare to a majority-class baseline: only +1 point

Q000948.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A trivial baseline that always predicts the majority class gets 90%, so the model adds only 1 point. Baselines show whether complexity is actually helping.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Production-ready: ignores the baseline.
• Regression only: baselines apply to all tasks.
• Complex model as baseline: defeats the purpose.

Key takeaway: always compare to a simple baseline.

Q000951.stem: A model gets a few requests per hour with long idle gaps. The payload is 2 MB, a 2-second cold start is acceptable, and the team wants to pay nothing when idle. Which option fits?

choices.text: An asynchronous endpoint kept at one instance
A real-time endpoint on a GPU instance
Batch Transform triggered per request
SageMaker Serverless Inference

Q000951.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless Inference scales to zero and bills per request duration, with occasional cold starts, which fits sporadic traffic with small payloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Real-time GPU: pays while idle.
• Batch per request: slow and awkward for requests.
• Async with one instance: pays while idle (async can scale to zero, but a fixed instance defeats that).

Key takeaway: sporadic traffic, no idle cost → serverless.

Q000953.stem: Every night, 50 million rows in S3 need predictions written back to S3 before 6 AM. No real-time access is needed. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

choices.text: A real-time endpoint invoked 50 million times
A multi-model endpoint for the nightly job
Serverless Inference invoked per row
SageMaker Batch Transform over the dataset

Q000953.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Batch Transform spins up instances, processes the whole dataset from S3 (with batching), writes results to S3, and shuts down, with no persistent endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Real-time endpoint: pays for always-on capacity and per-request overhead.
• Serverless per row: request overhead at huge scale.
• Multi-model endpoint: for many models, not bulk scoring.

Key takeaway: offline bulk scoring → Batch Transform.

Q000955.stem: A vision model must run on edge devices with ARM CPUs and limited memory, with lower latency than the framework runtime. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker JumpStart fine-tuning for smaller devices
SageMaker Neo compilation for the target hardware
SageMaker Clarify explainability
SageMaker Model Monitor

Q000955.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Neo compiles trained models into optimized executables for specific hardware targets, including edge devices, improving latency and memory use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: explainability.
• JumpStart: pretrained models.
• Model Monitor: production monitoring.

Key takeaway: hardware-optimized inference → Neo.

Q000959.stem: A custom inference container on SageMaker fails with 'container did not pass the ping health check'. Which TWO requirements must the container meet? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Serve predictions on POST /invocations
Write every prediction to Amazon Redshift
Run the container as the root user
Respond 200 to GET /ping when healthy
Expose a public static IP address

Q000959.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker hosting sends health checks to GET /ping and inference requests to POST /invocations on port 8080. The container must answer both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static IP: SageMaker manages networking.
• Redshift writes: not required.
• Root user: not required.

Key takeaway: BYOC hosting contract = /ping + /invocations.

Q000961.stem: A team wants to release a new model to a production endpoint gradually and roll back automatically if latency alarms fire, with no downtime. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A new EndpointConfig with deployment guardrails
Change the endpoint's IAM execution role
Delete the endpoint and create it again with the new model
Overwrite the model artifact in S3 in place

Q000961.explanation:
Why this is correct:
UpdateEndpoint with a new endpoint configuration and deployment guardrails (canary or linear traffic shifting with alarm-based rollback) shifts traffic safely while the old fleet remains available.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete and recreate: downtime.
• Overwriting S3: not picked up safely and no rollback.
• IAM role: unrelated.

Key takeaway: safe model updates → new EndpointConfig + guardrails.

Q000964.stem: A team wants identical SageMaker endpoints in dev and prod, reviewed changes before deploy, and easy rollback of configuration. Which practice fits?

choices.text: Define model, config, and endpoint in versioned IaC
Create endpoints manually in the console each time
Hardcode endpoint settings in application code
Use a one-off CLI script that is then discarded

Q000964.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Declaring SageMaker Model, EndpointConfig, and Endpoint resources in CloudFormation (or CDK) keeps environments consistent, lets change sets show diffs, and makes rollback a redeploy of a previous template version.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual console: drift.
• Hardcoded settings: not infrastructure management.
• Discarded script: not repeatable.

Key takeaway: ML infrastructure belongs in versioned IaC.

Q000965.stem: A custom inference image must be stored privately, scanned for CVEs, protected from tag overwrites, and pulled by SageMaker. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ECR with scanning and tag immutability
AWS Secrets Manager holding the image
Amazon S3 with the image stored as a tarball
AWS CodeArtifact as a private package and image repository

Q000965.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker pulls custom images from ECR, which offers scanning and tag immutability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 tarball: SageMaker doesn't run images from S3.
• CodeArtifact: language packages.
• Secrets Manager: secrets.

Key takeaway: container images → ECR.

Q000966.stem: A real-time endpoint's traffic grows fivefold at noon. The team wants instance count to follow load within limits of 2-10. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that resizes the endpoint
Application Auto Scaling target tracking
A Trusted Advisor recommendation reviewed weekly
A CloudWatch dashboard watched by the team

Q000966.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker endpoints scale through Application Auto Scaling, commonly with target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance and minimum and maximum capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance, not scaling.
• Weekly recommendation: manual and slow.
• Dashboard: observation only.

Key takeaway: endpoint scaling → Application Auto Scaling.

Q000969.stem: A bank requires that a SageMaker endpoint be reachable only from its VPC and that model containers can reach only approved resources. Which TWO measures address this? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Remove the IAM execution role
Turn on Model Monitor data capture
Invoke via an interface VPC endpoint
Enable SageMaker Neo compilation for the endpoint
Deploy in the VPC with security groups

Q000969.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running the model in your VPC with security groups controls what its containers can reach, and invoking the runtime API through an interface VPC endpoint (optionally with an endpoint policy and source-VPC conditions) keeps calls private.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neo: performance.
• No execution role: the model couldn't pull artifacts.
• Data capture: monitoring.

Key takeaway: private endpoints = VPC config + PrivateLink for invocation.

Q000970.stem: In the SageMaker Python SDK, which call actually provisions a real-time endpoint and what does it create?

choices.text: estimator.fit(...); trains and deploys
sagemaker.Session(); provisions infrastructure
model.deploy(...); creates config and endpoint
estimator.transformer(...); creates an endpoint

Q000970.explanation:
Why this is correct:
deploy creates the model (if needed), an endpoint configuration, and the endpoint with the requested instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• fit: trains only.
• transformer: prepares batch transform.
• Session: a client helper.

Key takeaway: deploy = real-time hosting.

Q000975.stem: An ML team wants a release flow: a commit triggers container build and tests, then a model pipeline run, then manual approval, then deployment. Which service ties the stages together?

choices.text: AWS CodePipeline orchestrating the stages
SageMaker Model Registry with approval events on its own
AWS CodeBuild on its own
SageMaker Feature Store

Q000975.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodePipeline orchestrates stages such as source, build (CodeBuild), SageMaker pipeline execution, manual approval, and deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Registry: stores models and approvals; it doesn't orchestrate.
• CodeBuild alone: runs builds, not a multi-stage release.
• Feature Store: features.

Key takeaway: multi-stage release orchestration → CodePipeline.

Q000976.stem: A pipeline must build the inference Docker image, run unit tests, and push to ECR on each commit, without managing build servers. Which service does this step?

choices.text: AWS CodeDeploy
AWS CodeBuild
AWS Config
AWS CodeArtifact

Q000976.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild runs builds and tests in managed containers, including docker build and push to ECR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy: deploys revisions.
• CodeArtifact: package repository.
• Config: compliance.

Key takeaway: build and test → CodeBuild.

Q000977.stem: A model-serving service on ECS needs blue/green releases with 10% canary traffic and automatic rollback on alarms. Which service performs the deployment?

choices.text: Amazon ECR
AWS CodeBuild with a deploy phase
AWS CodeCommit
AWS CodeDeploy (ECS blue/green)

Q000977.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy supports ECS blue/green with canary or linear traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild: builds.
• CodeCommit: source control.
• ECR: image storage.

Key takeaway: traffic-shifted releases → CodeDeploy.

Q000978.stem: An ML team releases models quarterly with a formal stabilization period and hotfixes, while another team deploys continuously. Which branching models fit each?

choices.text: Gitflow for both, since it supports pull requests
GitHub Flow for quarterly releases; Gitflow for continuous
No branching; commit directly to main for both
Gitflow for quarterly releases; GitHub Flow for continuous

Q000978.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gitflow's develop, release, and hotfix branches fit scheduled releases with stabilization. GitHub Flow's short-lived branches merged to main fit continuous delivery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: mismatches each cadence.
• Gitflow for both: heavy for continuous delivery.
• No branching: no review or isolation.

Key takeaway: match branching to release cadence.

Q000980.stem: A team wants its ML steps (processing, training, evaluation, conditional registration) defined as code, rerun reproducibly, with cached steps and lineage. Which service fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Studio notebooks run by hand
SageMaker Pipelines
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Feature Store

Q000980.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Pipelines defines ML workflows as a DAG of steps with conditions, step caching, parameters, and lineage tracking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Feature Store: features.
• Manual notebooks: not reproducible pipelines.

Key takeaway: ML workflow orchestration → SageMaker Pipelines.

Q000984.stem: Auditors ask which Git commit, dataset version, and pipeline run produced the model in production. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: Keep all models under one S3 key that is overwritten
Tag the model package with commit and run IDs
Skip version control because SageMaker tracks everything
Track this information in a shared spreadsheet

Q000984.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adding commit hash, data version, and pipeline execution ID as metadata or tags on the registered model package (plus lineage tracking) connects each deployed model to its sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overwritten key: destroys history.
• Nothing to configure: lineage still needs these identifiers recorded.
• Spreadsheet: disconnected and error-prone.

Key takeaway: traceability = IDs attached to the model version.

Q000985.stem: A demand model's accuracy drops slowly after a new competitor enters the market, though the input feature distributions look unchanged. What kind of drift is this, and how is it detected?

choices.text: Data drift; detected by input distribution checks
Latency drift; fixed by adding endpoint instances
Concept drift; monitor model quality against labels
Hardware drift; fixed by changing instance types

Q000985.explanation:
Why this is correct:
When the relationship between features and target changes while inputs look the same, that's concept drift. It shows up in model quality metrics once ground truth labels arrive.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data drift: input distributions change, which isn't the case here.
• Hardware or latency: unrelated to accuracy.

Key takeaway: inputs same, outcomes different → concept drift → model quality monitoring.

Q000989.stem: The team wants an alarm when p99 latency of a SageMaker endpoint exceeds 500 ms for 5 minutes, and another when invocation errors spike above normal patterns. Which fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch alarms, including an anomaly detection alarm
Amazon Macie findings
AWS Config rules on the endpoint
Trusted Advisor performance checks on the endpoint

Q000989.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker publishes endpoint metrics such as ModelLatency and Invocation5XXErrors to CloudWatch. Static alarms handle known thresholds, and anomaly detection alarms catch unusual spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration compliance.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: endpoint alerts → CloudWatch alarms.

Q000993.stem: A team wants to compare a challenger model with production on 10% of live traffic, measuring business outcomes before switching. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Two production variants weighted 90/10
Batch Transform on last month's data
Shadow variant with no responses returned
A second endpoint that clients choose randomly

Q000993.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An endpoint can host multiple production variants with weights. Real users receive challenger predictions for 10% of traffic, so business outcomes can be compared.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shadow: responses aren't served, so business outcomes can't be measured.
• Offline batch: no live outcomes.
• Client-side random choice: unmanaged and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: measure live impact → weighted production variants.

Q000995.stem: Data quality monitoring for an endpoint reports violations on every run, including for normal traffic. The baseline was created from a small, unrepresentative sample. What should be done?

choices.text: Re-baseline from representative training data
Disable monitoring until the model is retrained
Delete all constraints so no violations appear
Raise the monitoring schedule to every minute

Q000995.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Monitor compares captured data to baseline statistics and constraints. A baseline from representative training data (and reviewed constraints) makes violations meaningful.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable monitoring: loses protection.
• More frequent runs: more noise.
• Deleting constraints: removes detection entirely.

Key takeaway: good monitoring starts with a representative baseline.

Q000999.stem: A clinical model must be checked continuously for growing disparity in positive predictions between demographic groups, with alerts. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SageMaker JumpStart model evaluation run monthly
Feature Store online store queries
Clarify bias drift monitoring with Model Monitor
Ground Truth Plus labeling reviews

Q000999.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify integrates with Model Monitor to compute bias metrics on production data over time and raise alerts when they cross thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Feature Store: storage.
• JumpStart: pretrained models.
• Ground Truth Plus: labeling.

Key takeaway: bias over time in production → bias drift monitoring.

Q001000.stem: An endpoint's clients report slowness. Which set of CloudWatch metrics best separates model compute time from SageMaker overhead and shows whether instances are saturated?

choices.text: Invocations and TrainingJobStatus
ModelLatency, OverheadLatency, utilization
NumberOfHumanWorkersActivated
S3 bucket size of the model artifacts

Q001000.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ModelLatency measures time in the container, OverheadLatency measures SageMaker overhead, and utilization shows saturation. Together they locate the bottleneck.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invocations and training status: volume and training, not latency breakdown.
• Human workers: labeling.
• Artifact size: unrelated to runtime latency.

Key takeaway: split latency into model vs. overhead, and check utilization.

Q001004.stem: A security review must show who deleted a SageMaker endpoint last month and from which IP. Which source fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch endpoint metrics for Invocations
AWS Config conformance pack scores
AWS CloudTrail event history or trail logs
SageMaker Model Monitor reports

Q001004.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records SageMaker API calls such as DeleteEndpoint, with the principal, time, and source IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: performance, not who did what.
• Model Monitor: data and model quality.
• Conformance scores: compliance status.

Key takeaway: who called which API → CloudTrail.

Q001006.stem: Finance wants a list of SageMaker endpoints and EC2 instances that are idle or underutilized across accounts, as a starting point for savings. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Trusted Advisor cost checks (org view)
AWS Config conformance packs for cost rules
AWS CloudTrail Lake queries
Amazon Macie findings

Q001006.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks flag idle or underutilized resources, including SageMaker endpoints and EC2 instances, and organizational view aggregates across accounts. Compute Optimizer adds deeper rightsizing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance.
• CloudTrail Lake: API activity.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: idle resources → Trusted Advisor.

Q001008.stem: The ML platform must split SageMaker costs by project and environment, and restrict users to resources of their own project. Which practice supports both?

choices.text: Separate IAM users per project with no tags
Consistent tags: cost allocation and ABAC conditions
Enabling Model Monitor on every endpoint for usage reports
Encrypting resources with project-specific keys

Q001008.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Activated cost allocation tags break down costs, and IAM conditions on resource and principal tags restrict access by project.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Users without tags: no cost breakdown.
• Per-project keys: encryption, not cost or access by tag.
• Model Monitor: unrelated.

Key takeaway: tags drive both cost allocation and ABAC.

Q001012.stem: A training job fails with AccessDenied reading its training data in S3 and pulling a custom image from ECR, although the data scientist who launched it has access. Why?

choices.text: SageMaker uses root credentials, which are blocked
The job's execution role lacks S3 and ECR permissions
The training instance type can't reach S3 without a larger network size
The data scientist's IAM user needs more permissions

Q001012.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker jobs act with the execution role passed at launch (via iam:PassRole), not the caller's identity. That role needs S3 read and ECR pull permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Caller permissions: the job doesn't use them for data access.
• Root credentials: not used.
• Instance type: unrelated to authorization.

Key takeaway: jobs use their execution role.

Q001014.stem: A team attaches an S3 read policy to an IAM group and also wants SageMaker jobs to read the same bucket. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Roles are permission documents; policies are assumable identities
Policies can be attached only to roles, never to groups
Policies grant permissions; SageMaker assumes a role
The group's policy automatically applies to SageMaker jobs

Q001014.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policies are documents listing permissions and attach to users, groups, or roles. SageMaker jobs assume an execution role, so the permissions must be on that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed definitions: incorrect.
• Group policy applying to jobs: jobs don't act as group members.
• Policies only on roles: they attach to groups too.

Key takeaway: permissions live in policies; services act through roles.

Q001017.stem: A training job in a VPC must reach only an internal feature API on port 443 and S3 via a gateway endpoint. Which control restricts the job's network traffic at the ENI level?

choices.text: A KMS key policy on the output key
A SageMaker lifecycle configuration
A security group on the job's ENIs
An IAM policy on the execution role

Q001017.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups are stateful firewalls on the network interfaces SageMaker creates in your subnets, restricting outbound and inbound traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM: authorizes API calls, not network traffic.
• KMS: encryption access.
• Lifecycle configuration: notebook setup scripts.

Key takeaway: network paths → security groups; API permissions → IAM.

Q001019.stem: An MLOps pipeline builds images and deploys models across dev and prod accounts. Security bans long-term keys in pipelines. Which practice fits?

choices.text: One shared access key for every pipeline stage
Disabling IAM checks for the pipeline
An IAM user's access keys in the buildspec
Service roles assuming scoped cross-account roles

Q001019.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild and CodePipeline run with service roles that get temporary credentials and can assume narrowly scoped roles in other accounts for deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keys in buildspec: long-term secrets in code.
• Shared key: long-term and over-privileged.
• Disabling IAM: not possible or safe.

Key takeaway: pipelines use roles, not keys.
